OPENAPI BREAKING CHANGE CHECK · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Did this API version break existing clients?

Paste the OpenAPI 3.0/3.1 JSON document from before and after a change and this page reports exactly which differences would break an existing client — a removed endpoint, a parameter that became required, a narrowed type, a removed enum value, a request body that became required — separately from the non-breaking additions that happen every release.

Nothing is uploaded. Both documents you paste are read in this browser and never leave your device, and this tool makes no network calls of its own.

1. Paste both OpenAPI documents (JSON)

OpenAPI 3.0 and 3.1 are both understood, including specs that use $ref to shared components.parameters. Swagger 2.0 is detected and rejected rather than misread.

Paste a before and after OpenAPI document above and click Check.

Findings

KindOperationDetail

Prefer a CLI, or want this in your own CI?

Same logic, zero dependencies, one file:

python3 openapi_diff.py old.json new.json                    # human-readable
python3 openapi_diff.py old.json new.json --format json       # machine-readable
python3 openapi_diff.py old.json new.json --fail-on-breaking  # exit 2 only if a breaking change is found

Get openapi_diff.py from the repo — stdlib only, nothing to install, no network calls. --fail-on-breaking only fails the build on an actual breaking change, not on every routine addition, so it is safe to run on every pull request that touches the spec.

Common questions

Why not just read the diff of the two spec files?

A raw text diff of two OpenAPI documents shows every reordered key and reworded description alongside the one parameter that quietly became required. On a real spec with dozens of operations, the change that would actually break a client is a needle in that haystack. This tool ignores everything that does not affect the contract and classifies only what remains as breaking or not.

What counts as a breaking change here?

An operation (method + path) removed; a parameter that is new or became required; an existing parameter's declared type changed; an enum value removed from a parameter's schema, including a parameter newly restricted to an enum where it previously accepted any value, so a client could still send a value the new API no longer accepts; and a request body that became required where it previously was not. Everything else — a new optional parameter, a new endpoint, a widened enum, an enum constraint removed entirely — is reported separately as non-breaking.

Does this deep-diff my request and response body schemas?

No, not beyond a request body's own required flag. This is a shallow, structural diff of paths, operations, and parameter/request-body shape. A field added or removed deep inside a request or response body's JSON Schema is not reported. Treat a clean result as evidence about the surface this tool actually checks, not a full compatibility guarantee.

Does it upload my API spec anywhere?

No. Both documents you paste are read in this browser and never leave your device. An OpenAPI spec can describe an unreleased API surface, so this page makes no network requests of its own — pasting is the only way it sees anything.

Does it support Swagger 2.0 or YAML specs?

Not yet. This tool reads OpenAPI 3.0 and 3.1 JSON documents only. A Swagger 2.0 document is detected and explicitly rejected — its parameter and body shape differ enough that silently reading it as OpenAPI 3 would misreport rather than just refuse. Convert a YAML spec to JSON first with any OpenAPI tool's own export, or a YAML-to-JSON converter, before pasting it here.

More: how this compares to manually reading a diff of the spec files, or how this compares to oasdiff, the open-source CLI with a much deeper change catalogue. If a result surprised you, see why adding an enum to a parameter counts as breaking.

Everything runs in your browser. Both OpenAPI documents you paste are never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors, and the tool makes no network calls. Anonymous feature events (diff_run, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage and can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Diffing a build artifact instead of an API contract: SBOM Diff Check compares two CycloneDX/SPDX SBOM documents and reports added, removed, and version-changed packages, and SQL Migration Lock Check reads a PostgreSQL migration for statements that would lock or rewrite a live table — three different slices of the same "did this change, and does it matter" question, each over a different artifact a developer already has.

vs-manually-reading-the-spec-diff.html.text:
← back to the tool

This tool vs. manually reading the spec diff

The obvious first move when reviewing a new API version is diff old-spec.json new-spec.json, or scanning a pull request that touches the OpenAPI file. Both work, and both bury the one change that would actually break a client under everything else that changed for reasons nobody needs to review twice.

What each one is for

Reading the raw diff is correct and complete for reviewing every difference between two JSON documents: reordered keys, reworded descriptions, new examples, tag changes, all of it. Its limit here is one of attention, not correctness — a real spec has dozens of operations and hundreds of lines, and a parameter that silently became required reads exactly like the harmless reorder three lines above it.

This tool reads only the parts of the contract that can break a client — operations, parameters, and request-body requiredness — and sorts every difference into breaking or non-breaking before you look at a single line. It says nothing about a reworded description or a reordered tag list, because neither can break anything.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Did a required parameter get added, or an optional one become required?This tool's breaking list, immediately.
Was any endpoint removed?This tool's breaking list.
Did a description or example change?Neither tool flags this as breaking — read the raw diff if you need to review wording changes.
Did a field deep inside a request body's JSON Schema change?Neither tool catches this today — this tool's structural comparison stops at a request body's own required flag; a full schema-aware diff tool would be needed for schema-level coverage.
Is anything I paste uploaded anywhere?No, for this tool — everything runs in your browser. Pasting a spec into an online diff tool may log or cache it; check its own policy first if your spec is not public.

Common questions

What does a plain diff of two OpenAPI files actually show me?

Every difference between the two documents, with equal visual weight: a reordered object key, a reworded description, a new example value, and a parameter that just became required all look the same in a text diff. On a spec with dozens of operations, the one change that would actually break a client is easy to scroll past.

Is reading the raw diff ever the right call instead?

Yes, when you need to review everything that changed, not just what would break a client — a new example, an updated description, a reordered tag list, or a change deep inside a request or response body's JSON Schema that this tool's shallow structural comparison does not look at. A full-document diff or an OpenAPI-aware structural diff tool with schema-level coverage is the right choice for that review.

Can I just ask a teammate who wrote the change whether anything breaks?

You can, and for a small change that is often faster. The risk is the same as any manual review: the author already believes the change is safe, which is exactly the blind spot a mechanical, exhaustive comparison exists to catch, and it costs nothing to run alongside a human review rather than instead of one.

Does either approach tell me if the change is actually safe to ship?

No. Neither a raw diff nor this tool's structural comparison understands your clients' actual behavior — a client that never sends the removed parameter is unaffected by its removal, and this tool has no way to know that. Both only tell you what the contract itself declares differently; deciding whether that is safe to ship is a judgment call the two documents alone cannot make for you.

No warranty. This page and the linked tool apply a structural comparison to files you supply. They are provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied, and they are not a full compatibility audit. You are responsible for verifying anything here before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

This page names no specific product. "Manually reading the spec diff" describes a method, not any one company's product.

Nothing leaves your browser. The tool this page links to runs entirely client-side; nothing you paste is uploaded anywhere.

vs-oasdiff.html.text:
← OpenAPI Breaking Change Check

OpenAPI Breaking Change Check vs. oasdiff

Overlapping ground, very different depth and packaging. oasdiff is an installable, open-source Go CLI with 755 documented change rules reaching deep into request and response body schemas. This tool checks 12 of the most common operation, parameter, and request-body changes, on JSON you paste, free, with nothing to install and no network call of its own.

What each tool is for

oasdiff (github.com/oasdiff/oasdiff) is an open-source, Apache-2.0-licensed CLI written in Go, installed with go install github.com/oasdiff/oasdiff@latest, its Homebrew formula, a Docker image, or a pre-built binary from its releases page. It reads OpenAPI 3.0, 3.1, or 3.2 documents in either YAML or JSON, and its oasdiff breaking base.yaml revision.yaml command exits 0 when no breaking change is found and 1 when one is. Per its own documentation it recognizes 755 distinct kinds of change, breaking and non-breaking together -- including differences buried inside request and response body JSON Schemas, well past the operation/parameter level -- and can print the result as text, JSON, YAML, Markdown, or HTML. It also ships an official GitHub Action (oasdiff/oasdiff-action) that runs the same check on every pull request and posts a side-by-side review comment.

This checker does a narrower slice of that and nothing else: you paste two OpenAPI 3.0/3.1 JSON documents, and it lists every operation removed or added, every parameter that is new, removed, or newly required, every parameter type change or enum-value change, and every request body that gained or lost its required flag -- 12 change kinds in total. It does not read YAML, and it does not look inside a request or response body's schema beyond that one required flag. It runs entirely in your browser, needs no install, and makes no network call of any kind under any configuration.

Where to answer each question.
QuestionWhere to answer it
I need every documented kind of change, including ones buried inside a request or response body's JSON Schema.oasdiff -- 755 documented change rules cover that depth; this tool's 12 do not.
My spec is in YAML, not JSON.oasdiff reads YAML directly. This tool reads JSON only -- convert first.
I want an automatic review comment posted on every pull request that touches the spec.oasdiff's own GitHub Action is built for exactly that; this tool has none.
I just want to know if the two JSON files in front of me have an operation, parameter, or request-body change, right now, with nothing to install.This checker -- paste both, click Check, get the table.
I want this specific check to fail my CI automatically.Either: oasdiff's own exit code (0/1) in a CI step, or this tool's --fail-on-breaking for the narrower question specifically.
I don't want to install a Go binary or add a new GitHub Action just to check one pair of files.This checker -- it is a page, not a package.

The two are complementary, not competing: a team can run oasdiff in CI for full-depth coverage across every pull request and still reach for this tool the moment the question is "does this one pasted pair of JSON files have a common-case breaking change" without installing anything.

Run the free breaking-change check

Common questions

Should I use this checker or oasdiff?

They overlap on the common cases -- a removed operation, a parameter that became required, a narrowed type -- and differ sharply in depth and packaging. oasdiff is an open-source, Apache-2.0-licensed Go CLI (installed with go install, Homebrew, Docker, or a pre-built binary from its releases page) that reads OpenAPI 3.0, 3.1, or 3.2 documents in YAML or JSON and, per its own documentation, recognizes 755 distinct kinds of change -- breaking and non-breaking together -- including differences buried inside request and response body JSON Schemas. This tool checks 12 of the most common operation, parameter, and request-body-flag changes only, runs entirely in your browser on JSON you paste, and cannot read YAML or diff a body schema. If you need the deepest available diff, YAML support, or a GitHub Action that reviews every pull request automatically, oasdiff is the right tool. If you want a fast, no-install answer to the common-case question on two JSON files you already have open, this is the narrower tool for that.

Does oasdiff catch more than this tool does?

Yes, considerably more. oasdiff's own documentation lists 755 distinct recognized changes, spanning far past operations and parameters into request and response body schemas, headers, security requirements, and more -- ground this tool's shallow structural comparison does not cover at all. This tool implements 12 change kinds: an operation removed or added, a parameter that is new, removed, or newly required, a parameter's declared type changed, an enum value added or removed, a parameter newly or no-longer restricted to an enum, and a request body's required flag changing either direction. Every one of those also appears in oasdiff's catalogue; the difference is that oasdiff's catalogue keeps going well beyond them.

Why use a narrower browser tool if oasdiff already covers deep schema changes?

Two reasons this tool exists alongside it. First, oasdiff is a Go binary you install and then point at files on disk (or wire into CI via its GitHub Action); this tool is a page you open and paste two JSON documents into, which is faster when you just want one quick answer and have not set up a CLI or don't want to install a new binary for a single check. Second, a report spanning 755 possible change kinds is a different shape of answer than a short table naming exactly which operation, parameter, or request-body flag changed and how -- when the question is only the common-case one, this tool's narrower output is faster to read.

Does this tool read YAML specs the way oasdiff does?

No. oasdiff reads OpenAPI documents in either YAML or JSON. This tool -- both the browser page and the CLI script -- reads OpenAPI 3.0.x/3.1.x JSON only, and explicitly rejects a Swagger 2.0 document rather than misreading it. If your spec is YAML, convert it to JSON first with any OpenAPI tool's own export or a YAML-to-JSON converter before pasting it here, or use oasdiff directly on the YAML file.

Is this page affiliated with oasdiff or its maintainers?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by oasdiff or its maintainers. oasdiff is an independent open-source project, named here only to describe what this checker is and is not, using facts drawn from its own public documentation at oasdiff.com and its source repository at github.com/oasdiff/oasdiff.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime or that a URL will keep working.

Everything runs in your browser. The JSON you paste is never uploaded, and this page makes no live comparison against oasdiff -- it is a static page describing category facts sourced from oasdiff's own public documentation, not a live scan of any spec. We count only anonymous local feature events, never people or spec content, with an opt-out on the checker page. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

why-does-adding-an-enum-count-as-breakin.text:
← OpenAPI Breaking Change Check

Why does adding an enum count as a breaking change?

A parameter that used to take any string now only accepts three of them, and the checker calls that breaking — even though all you did was add a list of values. That reading is correct, and the same one rule explains it, and every other verdict this tool gives.

An "addition" that narrows is still a narrowing

Before the enum existed, the parameter accepted any value of its declared type: any string, any integer. Restricting it to ["standard", "express", "overnight"] does not add to what the API accepts — it shrinks it. Every value outside that list, including ones a real client could have been sending and getting a valid response for, is now rejected. The list itself is new; what changed for an existing client is that the API got pickier. That is what openapi_diff.py and this page are classifying as enum-added, and it is reported breaking for the same reason a newly-required parameter is: something that used to work can now fail.

This is a shallow, structural read of the parameter's own schema, not a request-by-request replay against real traffic — see how this compares to reading the spec diff by hand for what that trade gives up.

The one rule behind every verdict

Every change this checker reports, breaking or not, answers the same question: does this shrink what the API accepts from a client that has not changed, or take away something a client could already rely on? A "yes" is breaking. Everything that only adds an option, widens what is accepted, or lifts a restriction is non-breaking — even when the diff itself reads as an addition.

ChangeVerdictWhy
Enum added to a previously unrestricted parameterBreakingNarrows what the parameter accepts
Value added to an existing enumNon-breakingEvery previously-valid value still works
Value removed from an existing enumBreakingA value a client could send is now rejected
Enum constraint removed entirelyNon-breakingEverything that worked before still works, plus more
New required parameterBreakingA request that omitted it used to succeed
New optional parameterNon-breakingOmitting it still works exactly as before

Read this way, the checker has no special case for enums at all — it is the same narrowing-vs-widening test applied to a parameter's value set instead of its required flag or type.

Common questions

Why is restricting a parameter to an enum breaking, when I only added a list of values?

Because before the enum existed, the parameter accepted any value of its declared type — any string, any integer. Restricting it to a fixed list narrows that acceptance: every value outside the new list is a value an existing client could have been sending, and validly, that the API now rejects. The list is new, but what the API accepts got smaller, which is what the checker is classifying.

So is adding a value to an existing enum also breaking?

No, and this is the case most people expect: adding a value to a parameter that already had an enum is reported non-breaking. A client sending one of the old values keeps working exactly as before — the set of accepted values only grew. The breaking case is the opposite direction: a value that used to be accepted disappearing from the list, or the list appearing where there was none before.

What is the one rule behind every verdict this checker gives?

Does this change shrink what the API will accept from a client that has not changed, or take away something a client could already rely on? If yes, it is breaking. If the change only adds an option, widens what is accepted, or removes a restriction, it is non-breaking. A new optional parameter, a new endpoint, and an enum constraint lifted entirely are all widening moves, so all three come back non-breaking even though two of them are literally additions to the spec.

Does removing the enum constraint entirely count as breaking?

No — that direction is reported non-breaking. A parameter that used to accept only a fixed list and now accepts any value of its type still accepts everything an existing client was already sending, plus more. Nothing that worked before stops working, which is why the checker treats lifting a restriction as widening rather than narrowing.

Want the tool itself, or how it compares to oasdiff's much deeper change catalogue? See OpenAPI Breaking Change Check, or how this compares to oasdiff.
